title: Polarization signatures of mixed scalar - pseudoscalar ALP - photon couplings in intense laser pulses
authors: Musajan Kadir, Hong-Hao Fan, Ying Wu, Qi-Rong Wang, Bai-Song Xie
abstract: We investigate photon-to-axion-like-particle (ALP) conversion in a finite, linearly polarized laser pulse for a single ALP field with simultaneous scalar-type and pseudoscalar-type couplings to photons. Varying the collision angle between the strong pulse and the probe provides a continuous kinematic scan of the resonant ALP mass. For fixed kinematics in this setting, the scalar-type and pseudoscalar-type ALP conversion amplitudes interfere coherently, making both the photon-to-ALP conversion probability and the polarization rotation depend on the difference between the probe polarization angle $α$ and the coupling angle $θ_g$. Conversion is maximal at $|α-θ_g|=90^\circ$, where the polarization rotation vanishes, while the rotation magnitude peaks at $α-θ_g=45^\circ$ modulo $90^\circ$, where conversion is half-maximal. These complementary polarization-angle dependences provide polarization-resolved signatures of mixed scalar--pseudoscalar photon couplings.
summary: This theoretical study analyzes how mixed scalar and pseudoscalar couplings affect photon-to-ALP conversion in intense laser fields. The key finding is that the conversion probability and the resulting polarization rotation both exhibit a distinct, interference-driven dependence on the probe polarization angle. This provides a powerful, polarization-resolved signature for identifying the nature of the ALP coupling.
main_problem: The paper investigates the polarization signatures arising from the coherent interference of mixed scalar and pseudoscalar couplings between Axion-Like Particles (ALPs) and photons in intense laser pulses.
main_result: The conversion probability exhibits a polarization dependence proportional to $\sin^2(\alpha - 	heta_g)$, and the induced polarization rotation is directly related to the derivative of this conversion probability ($\Delta\alpha \propto -\partial P / \partial \alpha$).
method: The analysis uses a coherent interference approach, decomposing the probe polarization into a bright-dark basis to derive the conversion probability and the resulting polarization rotation.
model_or_system: The system involves a single real ALP field coupled to photons via both scalar ($g_s$) and pseudoscalar ($g_p$) interactions, driven by a strong, linearly polarized, pulsed laser background.
key_observables: Photon-to-ALP conversion probability ($P_{\gamma 	o \phi}$), polarization rotation ($\Delta\alpha$), and the dependence on the probe polarization angle $\alpha$ relative to the coupling angle $	heta_g$.
important_parameters: The coupling ratio controlled by $	heta_g$, the collision angle $	heta$ (for kinematic scanning), and the weak-conversion regime ($P_b \ll 1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis neglects dispersive birefringence and treats the strong laser pulse as an external, classical field (no backreaction).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the collision geometry and polarization conventions; one figure shows the dichroic rotation ($\Delta\alpha$) dependence on the polarization angle $\alpha$ for a head-on collision.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the fundamental interaction Lagrangian to derive the polarization-dependent conversion probability, then uses this probability to calculate the induced polarization rotation via differentiation, establishing a direct link between the two observables.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for using polarization-resolved measurements to distinguish between different types of fundamental couplings (scalar vs. pseudoscalar) in exotic particle searches, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and high-energy physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Collision geometry and polarization convention. The strong-laser quantities (k0, E0, B0) are shown in gold, while the probe quantities (k, E, B) are shown in blue. The strong laser propagates along +y, with its electric field polarized along +z, while the probe wave vector lies in the x–y plane and forms the collision angle θ with the laser. The angle α specifies the probe polarization relative to the strong-laser electric-field direction.

FIG. 3. Photon-to-ALP conversion probability Pγ→ϕ as a function of the probe polarization angle α and coupling angle θg for θ = 90◦, 120◦, 150◦, and 180◦. In each panel, mϕ = mres(θ), corresponding to ρ = 1. The white dotted and red dashed lines indicate the zero-conversion branch α = θg and the maximal-conversion branch α = θg + 90◦, respectively. The remaining parameters are given in Table I.

FIG. 4. Photon-to-ALP conversion probability Pγ→ϕ in the (mϕ, θ) plane for the maximal-conversion choice θg = 45◦and α = 135◦. The red dashed curve denotes the carrier-frequency phase-matching condition ρ = 1. The inset enlarges the head- on endpoint region. The remaining parameters are listed in Table I.

FIG. 5. Dichroic rotation for a head-on collision at mϕ = mres(180◦). (a) Signed rotation ∆α. The dashed branches at α −θg = 45◦modulo 90◦mark extrema of the rotation magnitude; adjacent branches alternate between negative and positive rotation. The dotted branches at α−θg = 0◦modulo 90◦indicate zero rotation. (b) Rotation magnitude |∆α|, for which the dashed branches mark the maxima and the dotted branches mark the zeros. The remaining parameters are listed in Table I.
